title: Normality Calibration in Semi-supervised Graph Anomaly Detection
one_liner: A student model learns what normal looks like by copying a teacher's score patterns and keeping normal shapes compact.
lead: When you only have a few labeled normal examples, a graph model tends to overfit to just those examples, missing what normal really means. GraphNC fixes this by having a student model copy a teacher's judgment across all nodes (labeled and unlabeled), then sharpens that judgment by keeping the internal representations of normal nodes tightly grouped, so anomalies stand out naturally.

problem.h2: Learning normality with only a handful of examples
paras: In a real graph, most nodes are normal (healthy users, legitimate transactions). You have a few labeled examples of normal nodes and want to spot the rare anomalies. The naive approach: train a model on only those few labeled normal nodes. But this backfires. The model learns the specific quirks of those few examples, not the general shape of normal.

The result: the model becomes very picky about what counts as normal. It flags many real normal nodes as anomalies (false positives) because they do not match the narrow training set exactly. The model has not learned the true pattern of normality; it has memorized a tiny slice of it.

callout.html: A model trained only on a few labeled normal examples overfits and flags many real normal nodes as anomalies.

steps.text: Pre-trained anomaly detector is locked; only the student learns.
Student’s score for each node drifts toward the teacher’s score (normal vs anomaly boundary).
Add small random noise to normal node representations, then measure how much the representation changed.
If perturbed representation drifts far from original, student loses a penalty—pulls them back together.
Normal nodes cluster tightly; anomalies drift away; decision boundary sharpens.

paras: The paper changes two things at once: the anomaly scores (the numbers that rank each node from most normal to most anomalous) and the internal representations (the pattern of numbers the model uses to describe each node). The student model learns to shift both to match the teacher.

hidden.name: Representation compactness
paras: This paper measures something called representation compactness: how tightly bunched the internal descriptions of normal nodes are. If all normal nodes have similar internal patterns, they form a tight cluster. If they are scattered, the cluster is loose. A tight cluster makes anomalies obvious (they fall outside it naturally). A loose cluster makes the boundary fuzzy, so anomalies sneak in.

The paper estimates compactness by adding tiny random perturbations (noise) to labeled normal node representations and checking if the representation stays close to the original. If a small noise causes the representation to drift a lot, the normal cluster is loose and fragile. If it stays put, the cluster is tight and stable.

heat.caption: Darker cells mean tighter representation (high compactness); light means loose. Perturbed versions stay close to original for normal nodes.

reads.html: Compactness is how close together normal node shapes stay when you nudge them slightly. Tight means anomalies stand out naturally. Loose means the boundary blurs and anomalies hide.
Perturbation-guided consistency loss enforces that perturbed and unperturbed representations of labeled normal nodes remain similar, minimizing the discrepancy via the loss function.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: learning from a broader teacher
paras: The core idea is that the teacher (pre-trained on some semi-supervised method) has already seen many nodes and learned a reasonable, broad definition of normal. It is not perfect, but it is broader than a model trained only on the few labeled examples. When the student copies the teacher’s scores across ALL nodes (not just labeled ones), it absorbs that broader view.

But copying scores alone is risky: the teacher makes mistakes on unlabeled data (it does not know which of those are true anomalies). So the paper adds a second lock: force the internal representations of labeled normal nodes to stay tightly grouped via the perturbation loss. This tightness acts as a shape constraint. A tight cluster for normal nodes means the decision boundary becomes crisp: anything inside the cluster is normal, anything outside is anomalous. This compactness also acts as a sanity check, because anomalies cannot easily fit into a tight cluster, they are naturally excluded.

stages.s: Graph with few labeled normal nodes and many unlabeled nodes
Teacher produces scores (soft boundary between normal and anomalous)
Student aligns its scores to teacher via ScoreDA loss
Perturbations added to labeled normal; student penalized if representation drifts
Tight normal cluster + clear anomaly boundary

math.words: Total training loss = ScoreDA (align student scores to teacher) + lambda * NormReg (keep perturbed normal representations close to original)
math.equation: L_total = L_ScoreDA + lambda * L_NormReg, where L_NormReg = mean(||h_i - h_i_aug||^2) for labeled normal nodes only
symbols: loss that pulls student score distribution toward teacher score distribution
loss that penalizes distance between original and perturbed normal representations
original representation (internal pattern) of labeled normal node i
representation of node i after adding small random perturbation
weight controlling how much to enforce compactness (higher = tighter cluster)
squared distance between two representations (how far apart they are)

worked.title: Worked example: two nodes over one training step
lines: Labeled normal node A: ScoreDA pulls its score from 0.3 toward teacher’s 0.8 (delta = 0.5). NormReg: original repr=[2.1,1.8], perturbed=[2.3,1.9]; distance=0.05, penalty with lambda=1.0 adds 0.05 to loss.
Unlabeled node B (unknown if normal): ScoreDA pulls its score from 0.6 toward teacher’s 0.4 (delta = -0.2). NormReg does NOT apply (not labeled), so no compactness penalty.
Total loss step 1: 0.5 + (-0.2) + 0.05 = 0.35. Model updates to reduce this, pulling A’s score down and compacting A’s representation.

math.note: ScoreDA spreads the student’s judgment across all nodes (labeled and unlabeled); NormReg keeps that judgment crisp by forcing labeled normal nodes into a tight cluster.

bars.h2: Performance on a simple graph benchmark

charts.title: Naive (trained only on few labeled)
charts.note: Model overfits to labeled examples; misses many normal nodes in unlabeled set.

charts.title: GraphNC (student + teacher + compactness)
charts.note: The teacher provides a broader, less overfit view of normality (reducing false alarms on the unlabeled set), and the tight cluster constraint makes the anomaly boundary sharp (increasing anomaly recall) because anomalies naturally fall outside the tightly grouped normal shapes.

items.html: If the pre-trained teacher misclassifies many nodes, the student copies those mistakes. The framework is only as good as the teacher it starts with.

items.b: Labeled normal nodes are not truly representative.
items.html: If the few labeled nodes are atypical (e.g., all from one subgroup), the tight cluster around them does not capture the full range of real normal. Anomalies from other normal subgroups will be flagged.

items.b: Perturbations do not match real noise.
items.html: If the random perturbations used during training do not resemble the kinds of noise or variation in real unlabeled nodes, the learned compactness may be fragile—it protects against the wrong kinds of drift.

items.b: Done right: start with a solid teacher, use truly random perturbations, and hold out a separate validation set to tune the lambda weight.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny graph with 50 nodes: 40 normal (tightly grouped in feature space) and 10 true anomalies (scattered). Use only 5 randomly sampled normal nodes as labeled training data. Train a baseline model on just those 5. Then train a student model (GraphNC) with a pre-trained teacher. Measure false-positive rate (how many normal nodes are wrongly flagged) on the 35 held-out normal nodes.
demo.metric_eq: False positive rate = (normal nodes flagged as anomaly) / (total held-out normal nodes); should drop from baseline ~55% to GraphNC ~15%
demo.closing: The demo must show that tight normal clustering (via NormReg) plus teacher alignment (via ScoreDA) cuts false alarms on unlabeled normal nodes by more than half.
